---
title: "Barnes-Hut and native acceleration"
description: "Run approximate t-SNE, choose neighbor affinities, and control native worker threads."
---

Most smallvis methods calculate interactions between every pair of observations. That makes them
convenient for experimentation on small datasets, but their time and memory requirements grow
quadratically. Barnes-Hut approximates repulsive interactions for t-SNE, HSSNE, and t-distributed
elastic embedding (TEE). Sparse neighbor affinities keep the attractive part of the calculation
sparse as well.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(smallvis)
```

## Run Barnes-Hut t-SNE

This configuration uses approximate nearest neighbors, a sparse neighbor graph, and two native
workers. Iris is small enough to run as a quick example; the configuration becomes useful when the
dense calculation is too expensive.

```{r barnes-hut, fig.alt="Barnes-Hut t-SNE embedding of iris, with species distinguished by color and plotting symbol."}
set.seed(42)
bh_fit <- smallvis(
  iris,
  method = "tsne",
  bh = TRUE,
  inp_kernel = "knn",
  nn = "approximate",
  n_threads = 2,
  perplexity = 30,
  theta = 1,
  exaggeration_factor = 12,
  stop_lying_iter = 250,
  Y_init = "spca",
  epoch_callback = FALSE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
species <- as.integer(iris$Species)
plot(
  bh_fit,
  col = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73")[species],
  pch = species,
  xlab = "t-SNE 1",
  ylab = "t-SNE 2"
)
```

Barnes-Hut requires two output dimensions. Smaller `theta` values open more cells and require
more work. Zero evaluates the repulsive sum exactly for the chosen input graph. The input kernel
and neighbor search still determine which affinities that graph contains.

The example uses binary k-nearest-neighbor affinities. Use `inp_kernel = "nngaussian"` for Gaussian
perplexity calibration over neighbors instead. The [input kernel and Barnes-Hut arguments](../reference/smallvis.html#arguments)
describe these controls.

The same controls work with `method = list("hssne", alpha = 0.5)` and
`method = list("tee", lambda = 0.01)`. Both require a sparse input kernel. They default to
`inp_kernel = "nngaussian"` and also support `"knn"`. HSSNE uses a heavy-tailed output kernel and
a global normalizer. TEE uses the t-SNE output kernel with a fixed repulsion multiplier.

## Accelerate a dense calculation

For dense t-SNE, `use_cpp = TRUE` enables native calibration and gradient calculations. It retains
the dense pairwise representation, so this speeds up a calculation without removing its quadratic
memory requirement:

```{r native}
native_fit <- smallvis(
  iris,
  Y_init = "spca",
  perplexity = 30,
  use_cpp = TRUE,
  n_threads = 2,
  epoch_callback = FALSE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
dim(native_fit)
```

Native acceleration covers selected calculations and methods. The specialized dense gradient
kernels use two output dimensions; other dimensions use the general R calculations for those steps.
`use_cpp = TRUE` therefore does not imply that every stage or every method runs in C++.

## Choose a thread count

`n_threads = 0` selects serial execution. Positive values control native worker threads in the
supported stages, including neighbor search. More workers can help larger inputs, but setup costs,
memory bandwidth, and work still performed in R limit the improvement. Numerical libraries can
also have their own thread settings.

Start with a modest worker count and measure the complete call on your data. Changing from dense
affinities to a sparse neighbor graph also changes the input problem, so compare those embeddings
as different approximations rather than interpreting the runtime alone.
